idea.text: Mixing concentrated sulfuric acid with water gives out a lot of heat. Add a little acid to a lot of water, slowly, and that heat spreads through all the water so nothing boils. Do it the other way round and the first drops of water boil instantly and spit acid.
idea.analogy: A spoonful of boiling water poured into a full bath barely warms it, but a bath's worth of heat dumped into one spoonful would boil it over. Always put the small, dangerous thing into the big, safe thing.

steps.title: Goggles on
steps.instruction: Concentrated acid destroys skin and eyes. Goggles on before anything else.

explore.if: wear my normal glasses instead of goggles
explore.then: Ordinary glasses leave gaps at the top and sides. Splashes come from any direction, so you need goggles that seal around your eyes.

steps.title: Water into the beaker first
steps.instruction: Pour about 50 mL of water into the beaker.

whatIf.wrong-target: Water goes into the beaker first so plenty of it is waiting when the acid arrives. Anywhere else, the beaker stays empty, and acid in an empty beaker has nothing to spread its heat through.
whatIf.order: Without goggles, one splash in the eye can cause serious, sometimes permanent, damage within seconds. That's why goggles go on before you open any bottle.
whatIf.rate: Pouring water fast mostly just splashes water, which is harmless here. But it's a bad habit for the acid later, where a splash can burn.
whatIf.overshoot: Too much water won't hurt anyone, but a very full beaker is hard to stir without slopping acid solution over the side.
whatIf.quantity: The amount of water changes the result: less water gets hotter (the same heat goes into less liquid), more water warms up less.

explore.if: use 25 mL of water instead of 50 mL
explore.then: The same heat goes into half as much water, so the temperature rise is roughly twice as big. The mixture could get close to boiling.

explore.if: use 100 mL of water instead of 50 mL
explore.then: The heat is spread through twice as much water, so it warms up only about half as much. Safer, but the acid ends up more dilute.

steps.title: Thermometer in
steps.instruction: Stand the thermometer in the water to watch the temperature.

explore.then: The dilution would still work, but you'd have no evidence that heat was given out. Measuring turns a feeling into data.

steps.title: Measure 5 mL of acid
steps.instruction: Pour 5 mL of concentrated acid into the measuring cylinder, very slowly.

whatIf.wrong-target: Pouring straight from the big bottle, you cannot tell how much went in, and it all lands at once: the water jumps by tens of degrees in seconds. Measuring a small, known amount in the cylinder first keeps the heat under control.
whatIf.order: Without goggles, one splash in the eye can cause serious, sometimes permanent, damage within seconds. That's why goggles go on before you open any bottle.
whatIf.rate: Concentrated acid poured fast glugs and splashes, and every splash is a drop that can burn through skin and clothes. Keep the flow under 1.5 mL/s.
whatIf.overshoot: Too much acid means more heat when it goes into the water. Doubling the acid roughly doubles the temperature rise.
whatIf.quantity: The amount of acid sets how much heat is given out: more acid makes a hotter mixture, less acid a cooler but more dilute one.

explore.if: pour the acid straight from the bottle into the beaker
explore.then: You lose control of both the amount and the speed. Measuring into a small cylinder first means you know exactly how much goes in, and can add it slowly.

explore.if: use 10 mL of acid instead of 5 mL
explore.then: Twice the acid gives out about twice the heat into the same water, so the temperature rise roughly doubles. Added quickly, that's hot enough to spit.

steps.title: Acid into water, slowly
steps.instruction: Pour the acid slowly into the water down a glass rod, stirring all the time.

whatIf.order: Acid first and water on top is the dangerous order: the water floats on the dense acid and boils the moment it touches it, spitting hot acid out of the beaker. The water must already be in the beaker.
whatIf.rate: Pouring concentrated acid quickly releases a burst of heat in one spot. The water there can boil and spit acid before the heat has time to spread. Under 1 mL/s lets it spread.
whatIf.no-mixing: Without stirring, the heavy acid sinks and makes a hot layer at the bottom. Stirring shares the heat through all the water so no spot gets hot enough to boil.
whatIf.overshoot: More acid than planned means more heat in the same water: a bigger temperature rise and a stronger final solution.
whatIf.quantity: A different amount of acid changes the result: more acid, hotter and stronger; less acid, cooler and weaker.
whatIf.water-into-acid: In a real lab, water poured onto concentrated sulfuric acid boils the instant it touches, throwing out droplets of hot, concentrated acid. People are badly burned this way. Always acid into water, never water into acid.

explore.if: pour the water into the acid instead
explore.then: The water floats on top of the dense acid and boils on contact, spraying hot acid. It's the classic lab accident this experiment teaches you to avoid.
The acid sinks and heats one layer at the bottom strongly. Stirring spreads the heat so the whole beaker warms evenly.

explore.if: stand the beaker in an ice bath first
explore.then: The ice soaks up heat as it is given out, so the temperature rises less. Chemists do this when they dilute large amounts of acid.

steps.title: Read the temperature
steps.instruction: Read the thermometer. How much did it warm up?

whatIf.reading: Reading from above or below eye level shifts the number you see (parallax). Bend down so your eye is level with the bottom of the curved surface, the meniscus.
whatIf.order: Read the temperature after the acid has gone in. Before that you're only measuring room-temperature water.

explore.then: The beaker loses heat to the air, so the reading drifts back towards room temperature. Read soon after mixing to catch the biggest rise.

safe-1.text: Concentrated acid is the most dangerous thing on this bench.

safe-2.text: Drag the goggles onto your face icon before you touch anything.

order-1.text: Which goes in the beaker first: the big volume of water or the small volume of acid?

order-2.text: Always water first, then add the acid to it. Remember: "Do what you oughta, add acid to water."

order-3.text: Watch: water first, then acid down the rod.

temp-1.text: Diluting acid gives out heat. How will you measure it?

temp-2.text: Drag the thermometer into the beaker, then open its reading lens.

slow-1.text: Concentrated acid is thick and heavy. What happens if it splashes?

slow-2.text: Barely tilt: keep the pour-rate gauge green, under 1 mL/s, and stir as you pour.

slow-3.text: Watch a slow pour down the rod.

observations.whatHappened: The water warmed by several degrees as the acid went in, but nothing spat because the heat spread through the large volume of water.
observations.why: Diluting concentrated sulfuric acid releases a lot of heat. Acid poured into water sinks, because it is denser, and mixes, so the heat spreads through all the water. Water poured onto acid floats on top and boils on contact, spraying hot acid.
realWorld: Why lab technicians store acids low down
Chemical burns first aid: lots of running water

prompts.question: Why must acid go into water, not water into acid?
choices: Water floats on acid and boils on contact, spitting acid
prompts.explain: The heat released boils a small amount of water floating on top, which spatters hot acid.

prompts.question: Diluting concentrated acid is...
choices: Only a physical change with no energy change
prompts.explain: It releases heat, so it is exothermic.

safety.title: Stop: water added to concentrated acid
safety.message: The water boiled on contact and sprayed hot acid. In a real lab this causes serious burns. Always put the water in first and add acid to it slowly.

captions.text: Goggles on before touching concentrated acid.
captions.why: Concentrated sulfuric acid is corrosive: it destroys skin and eyes within seconds.
captions.safety: Eye protection goes on first because splashes happen without warning, and eyes cannot heal the way skin does.

captions.text: Water goes into the beaker FIRST.
captions.why: The water is there to soak up the heat. The more water waiting in the beaker, the smaller its temperature rise.
captions.safety: With plenty of water already in place, every drop of acid lands in a big volume of water.

captions.text: Thermometer in, to watch the temperature.
captions.why: Diluting acid is exothermic: it gives out heat energy. The thermometer turns 'it got warm' into a number.

captions.text: Measure 5 mL of acid, very slowly.
captions.why: Concentrated acid is thick and dense (about 1.8 g per mL, almost twice as heavy as water), so it glugs if you tip it fast.
captions.safety: A slow pour means no splashes, and a small measured volume keeps the heat released small too.

captions.text: Acid into water, slowly, stirring all the time.
captions.why: The dense acid sinks and mixes into the water, so the heat is shared by all 50 mL. Stirring spreads it even faster.
captions.safety: Water poured onto concentrated acid floats on top and boils on contact, spraying hot acid. Remember: do what you oughta, add acid to water.

captions.text: Read the thermometer: the water got warmer.
captions.why: The temperature rise shows the heat given out as the acid spreads through the water. More acid, or less water, would mean a bigger rise.
